newsitem.title: USA: Phelps Dodge eschews post-Sumitomo protection.
newsitem.headline: Phelps Dodge eschews post-Sumitomo protection.

text.p: Phelps Dodge Corp said it now has price protection covering only 25 percent of its first quarter output at 95 cents per pound strike price, and has no cover on production further forward.
"I would be surprised if they come in the money at all or in the money in any material way," Douglas Yearley, Phelps' president, chairman and CEO told Reuters.
"Puts have disappeared as an economic reality post-Sumitomo. I think there will be less protection, from puts at least, in the future," Yearley said.

Phelps claims to have pioneered the use of puts before "they were vogue" and recently cashed in some of its 1996 and 1997 puts for $15 million. No other price protection schemes were currently being implemented by the company.
"We have broadly had the philosophy of not taking away the upside from our shareholders," Yearley said.
But if the market moved into contango, it might "change the game".

Following the copper crash in the wake of Sumitomo Corp's announcement of huge losses for alleged unauthorised dealings, a huge volume of puts came into the money, forcing banks and other institutions to cough up large amounts of cash to producers who had bought them.
"I think there are going to be some changes made to the board (of the LME)." Such a change was recommended in the Securities and Investment Board's review of the exchange.
